# EAI CLI

## Install

```bash
npm install -g @eai-tools/cli
```

Or run without installing:

```bash
npx @eai-tools/cli init my-vertical
```

## What You Can Build

  
    Declare Object Types with properties, relationships, actions, and side effects. Schema-driven development with full validation.
  
  
    Create, read, update, delete, and query resources across your data model. Pagination, filtering, and cross-type queries built in.
  
  
    Send chat messages, stream conversations, upload and classify documents, and index content for retrieval-augmented generation.
  
  
    Automated CI/CD with GitHub Actions. Deploy to Azure App Service with a single command. Environment management built in.
  

## Quick Workflow

```bash
# Scaffold a new vertical application
eai init my-vertical
cd my-vertical && npm install

# Authenticate and sync environment
eai login
eai env pull --include-secrets

# Define your data model, validate, and publish
eai types validate
eai types seed

# Start developing
eai dev
```

# Installation

The EAI CLI (`eai`) is a command-line tool for building vertical business applications on the EnterpriseAI platform. It handles everything from scaffolding new projects to managing data models, deploying to the cloud, and interacting with AI services.

Before you install, make sure your machine meets the prerequisites below.

## Prerequisites

- **Node.js 20 or later** -- the CLI uses modern Node.js features that require version 20+
- **npm** -- included with Node.js
- **Git** -- required for scaffolding new projects from the Vertical Template

Check your Node.js version:

```bash
node --version
# v20.11.0 or higher
```

  If you are running Node.js 18 or earlier, the CLI will not work. Use [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm) or [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm) to install Node.js 20+.

## Install

Choose the installation method that works best for your workflow.

  
    Install the CLI globally so the `eai` command is available everywhere:

    ```bash
    npm install -g @eai-tools/cli
    ```

    This is the recommended approach for most developers. It puts the `eai` binary on your `PATH` so you can use it from any directory.
  

  
    Run the CLI without installing it globally:

    ```bash
    npx @eai-tools/cli init my-vertical
    ```

    This downloads and runs the latest version on the fly. Useful for one-off commands or if you prefer not to install global packages. You can use `npx @eai-tools/cli` in place of `eai` for any command.
  

  
    Install with Homebrew on macOS or Linux:

    ```bash
    brew tap eai-tools/tap
    brew install eai
    ```

    This installs the `eai` command and manages updates through Homebrew. Requires Node.js 20+ to be installed (Homebrew will install it as a dependency if needed).

    To upgrade later:

    ```bash
    brew upgrade eai
    ```
  

  
    Download the npm tarball directly from a GitHub Release:

    ```bash
    # Download the latest release tarball
    curl -LO https://github.com/eai-tools/eai-cli/releases/latest/download/eai-tools-cli-0.1.0.tgz

    # Install it globally
    npm install -g ./eai-tools-cli-0.1.0.tgz
    ```

    Browse all releases at [github.com/eai-tools/eai-cli/releases](https://github.com/eai-tools/eai-cli/releases).
  

  
    Clone the repository and build from source:

    ```bash
    git clone https://github.com/eai-tools/eai-cli.git
    cd eai-cli
    npm install
    npm run build
    npm link
    ```

    This registers the local build as a global `eai` command. Useful for contributors or if you need the latest unreleased features.
  

## Platform compatibility

| Platform | Supported | Notes |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| macOS (Apple Silicon) | Yes | Tested on macOS 13+ |
| macOS (Intel) | Yes | Tested on macOS 13+ |
| Linux (x64) | Yes | Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, Fedora 38+ |
| Linux (ARM64) | Yes | Raspberry Pi OS, Amazon Linux 2023 |
| Windows (x64) | Yes | Windows 10+, PowerShell or WSL recommended |
| Windows (ARM64) | Yes | Windows 11 on ARM |

**Required runtime**: Node.js 20.0.0 or later.

## Verify the installation

After installing, confirm the CLI is available:

```bash
eai --version
```

You should see output like:

```
0.1.0
```

You can also run `eai --help` to see all available commands:

```bash
eai --help
```

Expected output:

```
Usage: eai [options] [command]

Enterprise AI Platform CLI — scaffold, seed, deploy, and manage vertical applications

Options:
  -V, --version   output the version number
  -h, --help      display help for command

Commands:
  init [name]     Scaffold a new vertical application
  dev             Start local development server
  login           Authenticate with Entra CIAM
  logout          Clear stored authentication tokens
  env             Manage environment variables
  types           Manage Object Type definitions
  tenant          Manage tenants
  resources       CRUD operations on platform resources
  chat            AI chat operations
  docs            Document management
  deploy          Deployment operations
  verify          Verify platform connectivity
  doctor          Diagnose common issues
  whoami          Show auth status and tenant info
```

## Update

To update to the latest version:

  
    ```bash
    npm update -g @eai-tools/cli
    ```
  

  
    npx always uses the latest version. No update needed -- just run your command and it fetches the newest release automatically.
  

  
    ```bash
    brew upgrade eai
    ```
  

  
    ```bash
    cd eai-cli
    git pull
    npm install
    npm run build
    ```
  

## Uninstall

  
    ```bash
    npm uninstall -g @eai-tools/cli
    ```
  

  
    ```bash
    brew uninstall eai
    brew untap eai-tools/tap
    ```
  

Your project files and local configuration (`~/.eai/`) are not deleted when you uninstall.

# Quick Start

This guide walks you through the complete workflow of creating a vertical application, from scaffolding to running a local development server. By the end, you will have a working project connected to the EnterpriseAI platform.

  Make sure you have the CLI installed before starting. See the [Installation](/eai-cli/getting-started/installation/) guide if you have not set it up yet.

## The full workflow

1. **Scaffold a new vertical**

   Run `eai init` with a name for your project. The name must be lowercase kebab-case (letters, numbers, and hyphens).

   ```bash
   eai init my-vertical
   ```

   The CLI prompts you for configuration options:

   ```
   ? Vertical name (kebab-case): my-vertical
   ? Display name: My Vertical
   ? Description: My Vertical vertical application
   ? Tenant structure: Single tenant (most common)
   ? Include AI chat? Yes
   ? Include document management? Yes
   ? Auth provider: Entra ID CIAM (recommended)
   ```

   Once you answer the prompts, the CLI clones the Vertical Template, customizes it, and initializes a git repository:

   ```
   Creating My Vertical

   ✔ Cloned from eai-tools/Vertical-Template
   ✔ Updated package.json
   ✔ Generated .env.local
   ✔ Created Object Types scaffold
   ✔ Created deploy-demo.yml
   ✔ Generated CLAUDE.md
   ✔ Initialized git repository

   ✔ Created My Vertical at /Users/you/my-vertical

   Next steps:
     1. cd my-vertical
     2. npm install
     3. eai login — authenticate with Entra CIAM
     4. eai env pull — sync environment from cloud
     5. Edit src/eai.config/object-types.ts — define your data model
     6. eai types validate — check your types
     7. eai types seed — push types to platform
     8. eai dev — start local development
   ```

2. **Install dependencies**

   ```bash
   cd my-vertical
   npm install
   ```

3. **Authenticate**

   Log in to the EnterpriseAI platform using your Microsoft Entra ID credentials:

   ```bash
   eai login
   ```

   The CLI starts a device code flow. You will see a message like:

   ```
   Authenticating with Entra CIAM
   Tenant: eaidevmyentepriseai
   Client: your-client-id

   To sign in, use a web browser to open https://microsoft.com/devicelogin
   and enter the code ABCD-EFGH to authenticate.
   ```

   Open the URL in your browser, enter the code, and sign in with your Microsoft account. The CLI detects the completed login automatically.

   ```
   ✔ Authenticated as you@example.com
   Token expires: 3/10/2026, 2:30:00 PM
   ```

4. **Pull environment configuration**

   Sync your project's environment variables from Azure App Configuration and Key Vault:

   ```bash
   eai env pull --include-secrets
   ```

   ```
   ✔ Found 12 config values
   ✔ BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API = https://test-api.myenterprise.ai
   ✔ TENANT_MY_VERTICAL_ID = [from Key Vault]
   ✔ ENTRA_CLIENT_ID = [from Key Vault]
   ...
   ✔ Written to .env.local (12 variables)
   ```

   
     The `--include-secrets` flag resolves Key Vault references into actual values. Without it, secret values are left as placeholders. You need Azure CLI (`az login`) access to resolve secrets.
   

5. **Edit your Object Types**

   Open `src/eai.config/object-types.ts` and define the data model for your vertical. The scaffold includes a sample `Record` type to get you started. Replace it with your domain model:

   ```typescript
   // src/eai.config/object-types.ts
   export const objectTypes = {
     'my-vertical': [
       {
         name: 'Task',
         displayName: 'Task',
         description: 'A work item to be completed',
         properties: [
           { name: 'title', type: 'text' as const, required: true, indexed: true },
           { name: 'status', type: 'select' as const, required: true,
             defaultValue: 'open',
             options: [
               { label: 'Open', value: 'open' },
               { label: 'In Progress', value: 'in-progress' },
               { label: 'Done', value: 'done' },
             ],
           },
         ],
         linkTypes: [],
         actions: [],
         status: 'published' as const,
       },
     ],
   };
   ```

6. **Validate your types**

   Check that your Object Type definitions follow the platform schema rules:

   ```bash
   eai types validate
   ```

   ```
   Tenant: my-vertical
   ✔ Task — 2 props, 0 links, 0 actions

   ✔ All Object Types are valid
   ```

   If there are errors, the CLI tells you exactly what to fix -- for example, a property with an invalid type or a missing `displayName`.

7. **Seed types to the platform**

   Push your Object Type definitions to the platform:

   ```bash
   eai types seed
   ```

   ```
   ✔ Found 1 types across 1 tenant scope(s): my-vertical

   Tenant: my-vertical → abc123-def456
     ✔ Task (created)

   Result: 1 created, 0 updated, 0 failed
   ```

8. **Start development**

   Launch the local development server:

   ```bash
   eai dev
   ```

   Your application is now running locally and connected to the platform. Open the URL shown in the terminal to see your vertical in the browser.

## What just happened

Here is a summary of what each step accomplished:

| Step | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|-------------|
| 1 | `eai init my-vertical` | Clones the Vertical Template and customizes it for your project |
| 2 | `npm install` | Installs Node.js dependencies |
| 3 | `eai login` | Authenticates you with Entra CIAM via device code flow |
| 4 | `eai env pull` | Syncs configuration from Azure App Config and Key Vault |
| 5 | Edit `object-types.ts` | Defines the data model for your vertical |
| 6 | `eai types validate` | Validates your types against platform schema rules |
| 7 | `eai types seed` | Publishes your types to the platform |
| 8 | `eai dev` | Starts the local dev server |

## Useful commands while developing

Once your project is running, these commands help you iterate:

```bash
# Check what has changed between local and remote types
eai types diff

# List resources of a given type
eai resources list Task

# Create a resource from the command line
eai resources create Task --data '{"title": "My first task", "status": "open"}'

# Verify platform connectivity
eai verify

# Diagnose common issues
eai doctor

# Check who you are logged in as
eai whoami
```

# Authentication

The EAI CLI uses Microsoft Entra ID with CIAM (Customer Identity and Access Management) to authenticate you with the EnterpriseAI platform. Authentication is required for any command that communicates with the platform -- seeding types, managing resources, pulling environment configuration, and more.

This page explains how the authentication flow works, where tokens are stored, and how to manage your session.

## How it works

The CLI uses the **device code flow**, an OAuth 2.0 pattern designed for command-line tools and devices without a browser. Instead of opening a browser window directly, it gives you a short code to enter on a separate device or browser tab.

1. **You run `eai login`**

   The CLI contacts Entra CIAM and requests a device code.

2. **The CLI displays a code and a URL**

   You see a message like:

   ```
   To sign in, use a web browser to open https://microsoft.com/devicelogin
   and enter the code ABCD-EFGH to authenticate.
   ```

3. **You open the URL and enter the code**

   In any browser -- on your machine, your phone, or another device -- navigate to the URL and type in the code. Then sign in with your Microsoft account.

4. **The CLI detects the completed login**

   The CLI polls the Entra token endpoint in the background. Once you complete the browser sign-in, it receives your access and refresh tokens automatically.

5. **Tokens are stored locally**

   Your tokens are encrypted and saved to `~/.eai/tokens.json`. All subsequent CLI commands use these tokens.

  The device code flow is secure because the code is short-lived and single-use. Even if someone sees the code, they cannot use it after you have already authenticated.

## Logging in

Run the login command from any directory:

```bash
eai login
```

If you are inside an EAI project (a directory with `src/eai.config/`), the CLI automatically picks up your Entra client ID from `.env.local`. Otherwise, you can provide it explicitly:

```bash
eai login --client-id your-app-client-id
```

The full set of login options:

| Flag | Default | Description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| `--client-id <id>` | From `.env.local` | App registration client ID |
| `--tenant-name <name>` | `eaidevmyentepriseai` | CIAM tenant name |
| `--tenant-id <id>` | Platform default | CIAM tenant ID |
| `--scope <scope>` | `openid profile email offline_access` | OAuth scopes |

A successful login looks like this:

```
Authenticating with Entra CIAM
Tenant: eaidevmyentepriseai
Client: a1b2c3d4-...

To sign in, use a web browser to open https://microsoft.com/devicelogin
and enter the code ABCD-EFGH to authenticate.

✔ Authenticated as you@example.com
Token expires: 3/10/2026, 2:30:00 PM
```

## Token storage

Tokens are stored in `~/.eai/tokens.json`, encrypted with AES-256-CBC. The encryption key is derived from your system's home directory path, so tokens are tied to your user account on this machine.

The stored token file contains:

- **Access token** -- used for API calls to the platform
- **Refresh token** -- used to get a new access token when the current one expires
- **Expiration timestamp** -- when the access token becomes invalid
- **Tenant information** -- which Entra CIAM tenant you authenticated against
- **User principal name** -- your email or username

  You never need to manage these tokens manually. The CLI handles reading, refreshing, and storing them for you.

## Automatic token refresh

Access tokens have a limited lifetime (typically 1 hour). When a token is about to expire (within 5 minutes of expiration), the CLI automatically uses the refresh token to obtain a new access token. This happens transparently -- you do not need to run `eai login` again.

If the refresh token itself has expired (after extended inactivity), the CLI returns a `null` token and you will need to run `eai login` again.

## Checking your auth status

Use `eai whoami` to see who you are logged in as and the status of your session:

```bash
eai whoami
```

```
Authentication
✔ Logged in as you@example.com

  Tenant      eaidevmyentepriseai
  Tenant ID   50808ce0-f31b-4fd0-9861-74b83b8c112a
  Expires     3/10/2026, 2:30:00 PM
  Status      Active
```

If you run this from inside an EAI project, it also shows your project context:

```
Project
  App Name       my-vertical
  Environment    dev
  PublicAPI      https://test-api.myenterprise.ai
  Config Tenant  abc123-def456
  Workflow       wf-789
```

If your token has expired, you will see:

```
Authentication
⚠ Token expired. Run `eai login` to re-authenticate.
```

## Logging out

To clear your stored tokens:

```bash
eai logout
```

```
✔ Logged out. Stored tokens cleared.
```

This deletes `~/.eai/tokens.json`. You will need to run `eai login` again before using any authenticated commands.

## Working with multiple accounts

The CLI stores one set of credentials at a time in `~/.eai/tokens.json`. To switch between accounts:

1. **Log out of the current account**

   ```bash
   eai logout
   ```

2. **Log in with the other account**

   ```bash
   eai login
   ```

   When the browser opens, sign in with the different Microsoft account.

If you frequently switch between accounts, consider using different client IDs for different projects. The CLI picks up the client ID from each project's `.env.local`, so you can have multiple projects authenticated against different Entra app registrations.

## Troubleshooting

### "No client ID provided"

The CLI could not find your Entra client ID. Either:
- Run the command from inside an EAI project directory (one with `src/eai.config/`)
- Pass it explicitly: `eai login --client-id your-id`
- Set `ENTRA_CLIENT_ID` in your project's `.env.local`

### "Device code flow timed out"

You did not complete the browser sign-in before the code expired. The code is valid for a limited time (usually 15 minutes). Run `eai login` again to get a new code.

### "Token request failed"

The Entra CIAM tenant rejected the authentication. Common causes:
- The client ID is incorrect or does not exist in the Entra tenant
- Your account does not have permission to use this application
- The Entra tenant has conditional access policies that block device code flow

### Token file cannot be read

If `~/.eai/tokens.json` becomes corrupted, delete it and log in again:

```bash
rm ~/.eai/tokens.json
eai login
```

# Your First Vertical

In this guide, you will build a **Task Manager** vertical application with three Object Types -- Project, Task, and Comment. By the end, you will have a working data model with typed properties, relationships between types, and actions with side effects, all published to the EnterpriseAI platform.

This tutorial assumes you have already completed the [Quick Start](/eai-cli/getting-started/quickstart/) and are authenticated with `eai login`.

## What you will build

The Task Manager has three interconnected types:

- **Project** -- a container for tasks, with a name, description, and status
- **Task** -- a work item belonging to a project, with priority, assignment, and lifecycle actions
- **Comment** -- a note attached to a task, with author tracking and timestamps

These types are connected through relationships: a Project has many Tasks, and a Task has many Comments.

## Scaffold the project

1. **Create the vertical**

   ```bash
   eai init task-manager
   ```

   Answer the prompts:

   ```
   ? Vertical name (kebab-case): task-manager
   ? Display name: Task Manager
   ? Description: Task management vertical application
   ? Tenant structure: Single tenant (most common)
   ? Include AI chat? Yes
   ? Include document management? Yes
   ? Auth provider: Entra ID CIAM (recommended)
   ```

2. **Install dependencies and authenticate**

   ```bash
   cd task-manager
   npm install
   eai login
   eai env pull --include-secrets
   ```

## Define the Object Types

Open `src/eai.config/object-types.ts` and replace the scaffold content with the following three Object Types. Each section below explains what the type does and why.

### The complete definition

```typescript
// src/eai.config/object-types.ts

export const objectTypes = {
  'task-manager': [
    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    // Project
    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    {
      name: 'Project',
      displayName: 'Project',
      description: 'A container for related tasks',
      properties: [
        {
          name: 'name',
          type: 'text' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'Project name',
        },
        {
          name: 'description',
          type: 'text' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'What this project is about',
        },
        {
          name: 'status',
          type: 'select' as const,
          required: true,
          defaultValue: 'active',
          options: [
            { label: 'Active', value: 'active' },
            { label: 'On Hold', value: 'on-hold' },
            { label: 'Completed', value: 'completed' },
            { label: 'Archived', value: 'archived' },
          ],
          description: 'Current project status',
        },
        {
          name: 'owner',
          type: 'relationship' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'User ID of the project owner',
        },
        {
          name: 'startDate',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'When the project started',
        },
        {
          name: 'dueDate',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'Target completion date',
        },
        {
          name: 'taskCount',
          type: 'number' as const,
          required: false,
          defaultValue: 0,
          description: 'Number of tasks in this project',
        },
        {
          name: 'metadata',
          type: 'json' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'Additional project metadata (tags, labels, etc.)',
        },
      ],
      linkTypes: [
        {
          name: 'tasks',
          targetObjectType: 'Task',
          cardinality: 'one-to-many' as const,
          cascadeDelete: true,
        },
      ],
      actions: [
        {
          name: 'archive',
          displayName: 'Archive Project',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-admin' as const,
          validationRules: {
            requiredStatus: 'completed',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field' as const, field: 'status', value: 'archived' },
          ],
        },
      ],
      status: 'published' as const,
    },

    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    // Task
    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    {
      name: 'Task',
      displayName: 'Task',
      description: 'A work item within a project',
      properties: [
        {
          name: 'title',
          type: 'text' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'Short summary of the task',
        },
        {
          name: 'description',
          type: 'text' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'Detailed description of what needs to be done',
        },
        {
          name: 'status',
          type: 'select' as const,
          required: true,
          defaultValue: 'open',
          options: [
            { label: 'Open', value: 'open' },
            { label: 'In Progress', value: 'in-progress' },
            { label: 'In Review', value: 'in-review' },
            { label: 'Done', value: 'done' },
            { label: 'Cancelled', value: 'cancelled' },
          ],
          description: 'Current task status',
        },
        {
          name: 'priority',
          type: 'number' as const,
          required: true,
          defaultValue: 2,
          description: 'Priority level (1 = critical, 2 = high, 3 = medium, 4 = low)',
        },
        {
          name: 'assignedTo',
          type: 'relationship' as const,
          required: false,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'User ID of the person assigned to this task',
        },
        {
          name: 'projectId',
          type: 'relationship' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'The project this task belongs to',
        },
        {
          name: 'dueDate',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'When this task should be completed',
        },
        {
          name: 'startedAt',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'When work began on this task',
        },
        {
          name: 'completedAt',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'When this task was marked done',
        },
        {
          name: 'isBlocked',
          type: 'boolean' as const,
          required: false,
          defaultValue: false,
          description: 'Whether this task is blocked by an external dependency',
        },
        {
          name: 'tags',
          type: 'json' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'Array of tag strings for categorization',
        },
      ],
      linkTypes: [
        {
          name: 'comments',
          targetObjectType: 'Comment',
          cardinality: 'one-to-many' as const,
          cascadeDelete: true,
        },
        {
          name: 'project',
          targetObjectType: 'Project',
          cardinality: 'many-to-one' as const,
          cascadeDelete: false,
        },
      ],
      actions: [
        {
          name: 'start',
          displayName: 'Start Task',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-user' as const,
          validationRules: {
            requiredFields: ['title', 'assignedTo'],
            requiredStatus: 'open',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field' as const, field: 'status', value: 'in-progress' },
            { type: 'set_timestamp' as const, field: 'startedAt' },
          ],
        },
        {
          name: 'complete',
          displayName: 'Mark Complete',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-staff' as const,
          validationRules: {
            requiredStatus: 'in-review',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field' as const, field: 'status', value: 'done' },
            { type: 'set_timestamp' as const, field: 'completedAt' },
          ],
        },
        {
          name: 'assign',
          displayName: 'Assign Task',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-staff' as const,
          validationRules: {},
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_user' as const, field: 'assignedTo' },
          ],
        },
      ],
      status: 'published' as const,
    },

    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    // Comment
    // ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    {
      name: 'Comment',
      displayName: 'Comment',
      description: 'A note or update on a task',
      properties: [
        {
          name: 'body',
          type: 'text' as const,
          required: true,
          description: 'The comment text',
        },
        {
          name: 'author',
          type: 'relationship' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'User ID of the person who wrote this comment',
        },
        {
          name: 'taskId',
          type: 'relationship' as const,
          required: true,
          indexed: true,
          description: 'The task this comment belongs to',
        },
        {
          name: 'createdAt',
          type: 'date' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'When the comment was posted',
        },
        {
          name: 'isInternal',
          type: 'boolean' as const,
          required: false,
          defaultValue: false,
          description: 'Whether this comment is visible only to staff',
        },
        {
          name: 'attachment',
          type: 'file' as const,
          required: false,
          description: 'Optional file attachment',
        },
      ],
      linkTypes: [
        {
          name: 'task',
          targetObjectType: 'Task',
          cardinality: 'many-to-one' as const,
          cascadeDelete: false,
        },
      ],
      actions: [],
      status: 'published' as const,
    },
  ],
};
```

### Understanding the structure

Each Object Type has four main sections:

**Properties** define the fields on each resource. Each property has a `name`, a `type`, and optional attributes like `required`, `indexed`, and `defaultValue`. The available field types are:

| Type | Use case | Example |
|------|----------|---------|
| `text` | Strings -- names, descriptions, IDs | Task title, comment body |
| `number` | Integers or floats | Priority level, count |
| `boolean` | True/false flags | `isBlocked`, `isInternal` |
| `date` | ISO 8601 timestamps | `startedAt`, `completedAt` |
| `select` | Enum values with predefined options | Status field |
| `json` | Arbitrary structured data | Tags, metadata |
| `file` | File reference URLs | Attachments |
| `relationship` | Reference to another resource by ID | `projectId`, `assignedTo` |

**Link types** define relationships between Object Types. Each link has a `targetObjectType` and a `cardinality`:

| Cardinality | Meaning | Example |
|-------------|---------|---------|
| `one-to-many` | Parent has many children | Project has many Tasks |
| `many-to-one` | Child points to one parent | Task belongs to one Project |
| `one-to-one` | Single reference in each direction | Profile belongs to one User |
| `many-to-many` | Bidirectional collection | Tags on articles |

Setting `cascadeDelete: true` means that when the parent is deleted, all linked children are also deleted. In our model, deleting a Project deletes its Tasks, and deleting a Task deletes its Comments.

**Actions** define named operations with role requirements and side effects. When a user triggers an action:
1. The platform checks whether the user has the `requiredRole` (`tenant-user`, `tenant-staff`, or `tenant-admin`)
2. It validates the `validationRules` (required fields, required current status)
3. It executes the `sideEffects` in order

The three side effect types are:

| Side effect | What it does |
|-------------|-------------|
| `set_field` | Sets a property to a specific value |
| `set_timestamp` | Sets a date property to the current time |
| `set_user` | Sets a relationship property to the current user's ID |

## Validate the types

Run the validator to catch errors before pushing to the platform:

```bash
eai types validate
```

```
Tenant: task-manager
✔ Project — 8 props, 1 links, 1 actions
✔ Task — 11 props, 2 links, 3 actions
✔ Comment — 6 props, 1 links, 0 actions

✔ All Object Types are valid
```

The validator checks for:
- PascalCase naming on type names
- Required `displayName` on each type
- Valid property types and `select` options
- Valid link cardinality values
- Valid action roles and side effect types
- References to existing properties in side effects

## Seed to the platform

Push your validated types to the platform:

```bash
eai types seed
```

```
✔ Found 3 types across 1 tenant scope(s): task-manager

Tenant: task-manager → abc123-def456
  ✔ Project (created)
  ✔ Task (created)
  ✔ Comment (created)

Result: 3 created, 0 updated, 0 failed
```

If you run `eai types seed` again later after making changes, existing types are updated rather than duplicated.

  Use `eai types seed --dry-run` to preview what would be seeded without making any changes to the platform.

## Create resources

Now that your types are published, you can create resources from the command line.

### Create a project

```bash
eai resources create Project --data '{
  "name": "Website Redesign",
  "description": "Redesign the company website with new branding",
  "status": "active",
  "owner": "user-001"
}'
```

```
✔ Created Project a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
```

### Create tasks in the project

```bash
eai resources create Task --data '{
  "title": "Design homepage mockup",
  "description": "Create wireframes and high-fidelity mockups for the new homepage",
  "status": "open",
  "priority": 1,
  "projectId": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
  "dueDate": "2026-04-01T00:00:00Z"
}'
```

```
✔ Created Task f1e2d3c4-b5a6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
```

```bash
eai resources create Task --data '{
  "title": "Write content for About page",
  "status": "open",
  "priority": 3,
  "projectId": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890"
}'
```

### Add a comment to a task

```bash
eai resources create Comment --data '{
  "body": "The mockup looks great. Let us move to development.",
  "author": "user-002",
  "taskId": "f1e2d3c4-b5a6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890"
}'
```

## Query resources

### List all tasks

```bash
eai resources list Task
```

```
✔ 2 total — page 1/1
  a1b2c3d4 title=Design homepage mockup, status=open, priority=1
  f1e2d3c4 title=Write content for About page, status=open, priority=3
```

### Get a single resource

```bash
eai resources get Task f1e2d3c4-b5a6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
```

### Cross-type query

Query across multiple Object Types at once:

```bash
eai resources query --types Task,Comment --where '{"status": {"equals": "open"}}' --limit 10
```

### View the published schema

See all Object Types currently published for your tenant:

```bash
eai resources schema
```

```
✔ 3 published types
  Project — 8 props, 1 links, 1 actions
  Task — 11 props, 2 links, 3 actions
  Comment — 6 props, 1 links, 0 actions
```

## Compare local and remote

After making changes to `object-types.ts`, use `eai types diff` to see what would change:

```bash
eai types diff
```

```
Tenant: task-manager
  ✔ Fetching remote types...
  ✔ 3 remote types
  = Project — no differences
  ~ Task
    + property: estimatedHours (local only)
  = Comment — no differences
```

This shows you exactly which properties, links, or types exist only locally or only on the platform, before you run `eai types seed` to apply the changes.

## Start developing

With your types seeded and sample data created, start the local dev server:

```bash
eai dev
```

Your vertical application is now running locally with live data from the platform. The Vertical Template includes a UI that automatically renders pages for your Object Types, so you can start building custom views and workflows immediately.

# Object Types

Object Types are the foundation of every EAI vertical application. They define your data model declaratively -- what fields exist, how types relate to each other, what business operations are available, and what happens automatically when those operations run.

Think of an Object Type as a blueprint for a business entity like a "Patient", "Invoice", or "Inspection Report". You write it once in TypeScript, validate it locally, and push it to the platform.

## How it works

```
object-types.ts  ──→  eai types validate  ──→  eai types seed  ──→  Platform
   (local)              (check rules)           (publish)           (live)
```

You define Object Types in `src/eai.config/object-types.ts`. Each type has four parts:

1. **Properties** -- the fields on the object (text, number, date, etc.)
2. **Links** -- relationships to other Object Types (one-to-one, one-to-many, etc.)
3. **Actions** -- named business operations with role gates and validation
4. **Side Effects** -- computed values that run automatically when actions execute

## Defining an Object Type

Object Types are exported as a record keyed by tenant scope:

```typescript title="src/eai.config/object-types.ts"

export const objectTypes: Record<string, ObjectTypeDefinition[]> = {
  'my-tenant': [
    {
      name: 'Patient',
      displayName: 'Patient',
      description: 'A registered patient in the system',
      status: 'published',
      properties: [
        { name: 'firstName', type: 'text', required: true },
        { name: 'lastName', type: 'text', required: true },
        { name: 'dateOfBirth', type: 'date', required: true },
        { name: 'email', type: 'text', required: false, indexed: true },
        { name: 'status', type: 'select', required: true, options: [
          { label: 'Active', value: 'active' },
          { label: 'Inactive', value: 'inactive' },
          { label: 'Discharged', value: 'discharged' },
        ]},
      ],
      linkTypes: [],
      actions: [],
    },
  ],
};
```

  The tenant key (e.g. `'my-tenant'`) maps to the environment variable `TENANT_MY_TENANT_ID` in your `.env.local`. The CLI resolves this automatically when seeding.

## Properties (field types)

Every property has a `name`, `type`, and `required` flag. Some types accept additional configuration.

| Type       | Description                        | Additional options       |
|------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| `text`     | String value                       | `indexed`, `defaultValue` |
| `number`   | Numeric value (integer or float)   | `indexed`, `defaultValue` |
| `boolean`  | True/false                         | `defaultValue`           |
| `date`     | ISO 8601 date/datetime             | `indexed`                |
| `select`   | Constrained choice from options    | `options` (required)     |
| `json`     | Arbitrary JSON object              | --                       |
| `file`     | File attachment reference          | --                       |
| `relationship` | Reference to another resource  | `indexed`                |

### Property examples

```typescript
// Simple text field
{ name: 'title', type: 'text', required: true }

// Number with a default
{ name: 'priority', type: 'number', required: false, defaultValue: 0 }

// Boolean flag
{ name: 'isUrgent', type: 'boolean', required: false, defaultValue: false }

// Date field with indexing for fast queries
{ name: 'submittedAt', type: 'date', required: false, indexed: true }

// Select with constrained options
{
  name: 'severity',
  type: 'select',
  required: true,
  options: [
    { label: 'Low', value: 'low' },
    { label: 'Medium', value: 'medium' },
    { label: 'High', value: 'high' },
    { label: 'Critical', value: 'critical' },
  ],
}

// JSON for flexible/nested data
{ name: 'metadata', type: 'json', required: false }

// File attachment
{ name: 'attachment', type: 'file', required: false }

// Relationship to another resource
{ name: 'assignedTo', type: 'relationship', required: false, indexed: true }
```

  Select properties **must** include an `options` array. The validator will reject a select field without options.

## Links (relationships)

Links define how Object Types relate to each other. Each link specifies a target type and a cardinality.

```typescript
linkTypes: [
  {
    name: 'appointments',
    targetObjectType: 'Appointment',
    cardinality: 'one-to-many',
  },
  {
    name: 'primaryPhysician',
    targetObjectType: 'Physician',
    cardinality: 'many-to-one',
  },
  {
    name: 'emergencyContact',
    targetObjectType: 'Contact',
    cardinality: 'one-to-one',
    cascadeDelete: true,
  },
  {
    name: 'insurancePlans',
    targetObjectType: 'InsurancePlan',
    cardinality: 'many-to-many',
  },
]
```

### Cardinality options

| Cardinality    | Meaning                                      |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `one-to-one`   | Exactly one related resource                 |
| `one-to-many`  | This resource has many of the target type     |
| `many-to-one`  | Many of this resource point to one target     |
| `many-to-many` | Many-to-many relationship                    |

When `cascadeDelete` is `true`, deleting the parent resource also deletes linked resources.

## Actions (business operations)

Actions define named operations that users can perform on a resource. Each action specifies who can run it (via `requiredRole`), what validation must pass, and what side effects execute automatically.

```typescript
actions: [
  {
    name: 'submit',
    displayName: 'Submit for Review',
    requiredRole: 'tenant-user',
    validationRules: {
      requiredFields: ['firstName', 'lastName', 'dateOfBirth'],
      requiredStatus: 'draft',
    },
    sideEffects: [
      { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'submitted' },
      { type: 'set_timestamp', field: 'submittedAt' },
      { type: 'set_user', field: 'submittedBy' },
    ],
  },
  {
    name: 'approve',
    displayName: 'Approve',
    requiredRole: 'tenant-staff',
    validationRules: {
      requiredStatus: 'submitted',
    },
    sideEffects: [
      { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'approved' },
      { type: 'set_timestamp', field: 'approvedAt' },
      { type: 'set_user', field: 'approvedBy' },
    ],
  },
]
```

### Roles

| Role            | Description                                    |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `tenant-user`   | Any authenticated user within the tenant       |
| `tenant-staff`  | Staff-level user with elevated permissions     |
| `tenant-admin`  | Full administrative access within the tenant   |

### Validation rules

- **`requiredFields`** -- an array of property names that must be non-empty before the action can run.
- **`requiredStatus`** -- the current value of the `status` field that must match (if your type uses a status field).

## Side effects (computed values)

Side effects run automatically when an action executes. They set field values without requiring the caller to provide them.

| Side effect type  | What it does                                      |
|-------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `set_field`       | Sets a property to a fixed value                  |
| `set_timestamp`   | Sets a property to the current ISO 8601 timestamp |
| `set_user`        | Sets a property to the ID of the acting user      |

```typescript
sideEffects: [
  // Set the status to 'approved'
  { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'approved' },

  // Record when the action happened
  { type: 'set_timestamp', field: 'approvedAt' },

  // Record who performed the action
  { type: 'set_user', field: 'approvedBy' },
]
```

  The validator warns if a side effect references a field that is not defined in the type's `properties` array. Always define the target field first.

## Complete example

Here is a full Object Type definition for an inspection report workflow:

```typescript title="src/eai.config/object-types.ts"

export const objectTypes: Record<string, ObjectTypeDefinition[]> = {
  'quality-control': [
    {
      name: 'InspectionReport',
      displayName: 'Inspection Report',
      description: 'Quality inspection report for manufacturing line items',
      status: 'published',
      properties: [
        { name: 'title', type: 'text', required: true },
        { name: 'description', type: 'text', required: false },
        { name: 'inspectionDate', type: 'date', required: true, indexed: true },
        { name: 'severity', type: 'select', required: true, options: [
          { label: 'Minor', value: 'minor' },
          { label: 'Major', value: 'major' },
          { label: 'Critical', value: 'critical' },
        ]},
        { name: 'status', type: 'select', required: true, options: [
          { label: 'Draft', value: 'draft' },
          { label: 'Submitted', value: 'submitted' },
          { label: 'Approved', value: 'approved' },
          { label: 'Rejected', value: 'rejected' },
        ]},
        { name: 'findings', type: 'json', required: false },
        { name: 'photos', type: 'file', required: false },
        { name: 'submittedAt', type: 'date', required: false },
        { name: 'submittedBy', type: 'text', required: false },
        { name: 'approvedAt', type: 'date', required: false },
        { name: 'approvedBy', type: 'text', required: false },
      ],
      linkTypes: [
        {
          name: 'productionLine',
          targetObjectType: 'ProductionLine',
          cardinality: 'many-to-one',
        },
        {
          name: 'correctiveActions',
          targetObjectType: 'CorrectiveAction',
          cardinality: 'one-to-many',
          cascadeDelete: true,
        },
      ],
      actions: [
        {
          name: 'submit',
          displayName: 'Submit Report',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-user',
          validationRules: {
            requiredFields: ['title', 'inspectionDate', 'severity'],
            requiredStatus: 'draft',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'submitted' },
            { type: 'set_timestamp', field: 'submittedAt' },
            { type: 'set_user', field: 'submittedBy' },
          ],
        },
        {
          name: 'approve',
          displayName: 'Approve Report',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-staff',
          validationRules: {
            requiredStatus: 'submitted',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'approved' },
            { type: 'set_timestamp', field: 'approvedAt' },
            { type: 'set_user', field: 'approvedBy' },
          ],
        },
        {
          name: 'reject',
          displayName: 'Reject Report',
          requiredRole: 'tenant-staff',
          validationRules: {
            requiredStatus: 'submitted',
          },
          sideEffects: [
            { type: 'set_field', field: 'status', value: 'rejected' },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
```

## Validation rules

The CLI validates your Object Types before publishing. Run validation locally:

```bash
eai types validate
```

The validator checks:

| Rule                                 | Severity |
|--------------------------------------|----------|
| Name must be PascalCase              | Error    |
| `displayName` is required            | Error    |
| `status` must be `draft`, `published`, or `deprecated` | Error |
| No duplicate property names          | Error    |
| Property type must be a valid type   | Error    |
| Select properties must have `options`| Error    |
| Link `targetObjectType` is required  | Error    |
| Link `cardinality` must be valid     | Error    |
| Action `name` is required            | Error    |
| Action `requiredRole` must be valid  | Error    |
| Side effect `type` must be valid     | Error    |
| Side effect references unknown field | Warning  |
| Non-select property has `options`    | Warning  |

## CLI commands

1. **Validate** your types locally:
   ```bash
   eai types validate
   ```

2. **Seed** (push) types to the platform:
   ```bash
   eai types seed
   ```
   Use `--dry-run` to preview without making changes:
   ```bash
   eai types seed --dry-run
   ```

3. **Diff** local vs. remote types:
   ```bash
   eai types diff
   ```

4. **Pull** remote types into a generated TypeScript file:
   ```bash
   eai types pull
   ```
   Output goes to `src/eai.config/object-types.generated.ts` by default.

### Seeding to a specific tenant

If your `object-types.ts` exports multiple tenant scopes, you can seed a specific one:

```bash
eai types seed --tenant-key quality-control
```

## Status lifecycle

Object Types have a status that controls their visibility on the platform:

```
draft  ──→  published  ──→  deprecated
```

- **`draft`** -- visible only in development, not queryable via the resources API.
- **`published`** -- live on the platform, resources can be created against this type.
- **`deprecated`** -- existing resources are still accessible, but new resources cannot be created.

## Next steps

- [Resources](/eai-cli/guides/resources/) -- create, query, and manage resources based on your Object Types
- [AI Features](/eai-cli/guides/ai-features/) -- integrate AI workflows with your data model
- [Security](/eai-cli/guides/security/) -- understand how roles and actions interact with access control

# Resources

Resources are instances of your [Object Types](/eai-cli/guides/object-types/). If an Object Type is "Patient", then a resource is a specific patient record. The `eai resources` command gives you full CRUD operations, querying, filtering, and cross-type queries from the terminal.

## How it works

```
eai resources create Patient --data '{...}'
                 │
                 ▼
         Platform API (/v3/resources)
                 │
                 ▼
       Resource stored with tenant isolation
```

The CLI reads your `BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API` and tenant ID from `.env.local`, attaches your Bearer token, and calls the Platform API. Every resource is scoped to a tenant -- you never see resources from other tenants.

## Creating resources

Create a resource by specifying the Object Type name and providing data as JSON:

```bash
eai resources create Patient --data '{
  "firstName": "Jane",
  "lastName": "Doe",
  "dateOfBirth": "1990-03-15",
  "email": "jane.doe@example.com",
  "status": "active"
}'
```

You can also load data from a file:

```bash
eai resources create Patient --file ./data/patient.json
```

```json title="data/patient.json"
{
  "firstName": "Jane",
  "lastName": "Doe",
  "dateOfBirth": "1990-03-15",
  "email": "jane.doe@example.com",
  "status": "active"
}
```

The CLI returns the created resource ID on success:

```
✔ Created Patient 3f8a2b1c
```

## Listing resources

List all resources of a given type:

```bash
eai resources list Patient
```

Output:

```
✔ 47 total — page 1/3
  3f8a2b1c firstName=Jane, lastName=Doe, status=active
  a1b2c3d4 firstName=John, lastName=Smith, status=active
  ...
```

### Pagination

Control page size and page number:

```bash
# Show 50 items per page
eai resources list Patient --limit 50

# Go to page 2
eai resources list Patient --page 2 --limit 50
```

### Sorting

Sort by any field. Prefix with `-` for descending order:

```bash
# Sort by creation date, newest first (default)
eai resources list Patient --sort -created_at

# Sort by last name, ascending
eai resources list Patient --sort lastName

# Sort by status descending
eai resources list Patient --sort -status
```

### JSON output

Get raw JSON for piping to other tools:

```bash
eai resources list Patient --json
```

```json
{
  "docs": [
    {
      "id": "3f8a2b1c-...",
      "data": {
        "firstName": "Jane",
        "lastName": "Doe",
        "status": "active"
      },
      "created_at": "2025-01-15T10:30:00Z",
      "version": 1
    }
  ],
  "totalDocs": 47,
  "page": 1,
  "totalPages": 3
}
```

  Combine `--json` with tools like `jq` for powerful filtering: `eai resources list Patient --json | jq '.docs[] | .data.email'`

## Getting a single resource

Fetch a resource by its type and ID:

```bash
eai resources get Patient 3f8a2b1c-1234-5678-abcd-ef0123456789
```

Add `--json` for raw output:

```bash
eai resources get Patient 3f8a2b1c-1234-5678-abcd-ef0123456789 --json
```

## Updating resources

Update specific fields on an existing resource:

```bash
eai resources update Patient 3f8a2b1c-1234-5678-abcd-ef0123456789 \
  --data '{"email": "jane.new@example.com"}'
```

### Optimistic locking

Resources use version-based optimistic locking. By default, the CLI fetches the current version automatically before updating. You can specify the version explicitly to guard against concurrent edits:

```bash
eai resources update Patient 3f8a2b1c --data '{"status": "inactive"}' --version 3
```

If the version does not match the current version on the platform, the update is rejected. This prevents one user from overwriting another user's changes.

## Deleting resources

Delete a resource by type and ID:

```bash
eai resources delete Patient 3f8a2b1c-1234-5678-abcd-ef0123456789
```

The CLI prompts for confirmation. Use `--force` to skip the prompt (useful in scripts):

```bash
eai resources delete Patient 3f8a2b1c --force
```

  Deletion is permanent. If the Object Type has links with `cascadeDelete: true`, linked resources will also be deleted.

## Cross-type queries

Query across multiple Object Types at once using `eai resources query`:

```bash
eai resources query --types Patient,Appointment --limit 10
```

### Filtering with --where

Pass filter conditions as a JSON object:

```bash
eai resources query \
  --types Patient \
  --where '{"status": {"equals": "active"}}'
```

Supported filter operators:

| Operator        | Example                                    | Description           |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| `equals`        | `{"status": {"equals": "active"}}`         | Exact match           |
| `not_equals`    | `{"status": {"not_equals": "inactive"}}`   | Not equal             |
| `contains`      | `{"name": {"contains": "doe"}}`            | Substring match       |
| `greater_than`  | `{"age": {"greater_than": 18}}`            | Numeric comparison    |
| `less_than`     | `{"age": {"less_than": 65}}`               | Numeric comparison    |

### Combining filters

```bash
eai resources query \
  --types InspectionReport \
  --where '{
    "severity": {"equals": "critical"},
    "status": {"equals": "submitted"}
  }' \
  --limit 50
```

## Viewing the schema

See all published Object Types for your tenant:

```bash
eai resources schema
```

Output:

```
✔ 5 published types
  Patient — 8 props, 2 links, 3 actions
  Appointment — 5 props, 1 links, 2 actions
  Physician — 4 props, 0 links, 0 actions
  InsurancePlan — 6 props, 0 links, 1 actions
  Contact — 3 props, 0 links, 0 actions
```

## Executing actions

Actions defined on Object Types can be executed via the Platform API. While the CLI does not currently expose a dedicated `eai resources action` subcommand, you can call actions through the API:

```bash
curl -X POST "${BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API}/v3/resources/${TENANT_ID}/Patient/${RESOURCE_ID}/actions/submit" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(eai whoami --token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"params": {}}'
```

  Action execution respects the `requiredRole` and `validationRules` defined on the Object Type. If the acting user lacks the required role or validation fails, the action is rejected.

## Common workflows

### Bulk creation from a directory of JSON files

```bash
for file in data/patients/*.json; do
  eai resources create Patient --file "$file"
done
```

### Export all resources to a file

```bash
eai resources list Patient --limit 1000 --json > patients-export.json
```

### Filter and count

```bash
eai resources query \
  --types Patient \
  --where '{"status": {"equals": "active"}}' \
  --json | jq '.docs | length'
```

## Command reference

| Command                          | Description                        |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `eai resources list <type>`      | List resources with pagination     |
| `eai resources get <type> <id>`  | Get a single resource              |
| `eai resources create <type>`    | Create a new resource              |
| `eai resources update <type> <id>` | Update an existing resource      |
| `eai resources delete <type> <id>` | Delete a resource                |
| `eai resources query`            | Cross-type query with filters      |
| `eai resources schema`           | Show published Object Types        |

- [Object Types](/eai-cli/guides/object-types/) -- define the data model that resources are based on
- [AI Features](/eai-cli/guides/ai-features/) -- combine resources with AI chat and document processing

# Environment

EAI projects use environment variables to configure API endpoints, tenant IDs, authentication credentials, and feature flags. The `eai env` command syncs these values between Azure App Configuration (with Key Vault for secrets) and your local `.env.local` file.

## How it works

```
Azure App Config + Key Vault
         │
    eai env pull
         │
         ▼
     .env.local  ←  Your local development config
         │
    eai env push
         │
         ▼
Azure App Config (admin only)
```

Configuration is stored centrally in Azure App Configuration. Secrets (API keys, connection strings, auth credentials) are stored in Azure Key Vault and referenced from App Config. The CLI resolves both in a single `pull` operation.

## Pulling configuration

Sync cloud configuration to your local `.env.local`:

```bash
eai env pull
```

This connects to Azure App Configuration, fetches all key-value pairs for your application label, and writes them to `.env.local` at your project root.

Output:

```
✔ Found 12 config values
✔ BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API = https://api.example.com
✔ NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME = trial-portal
✔ TENANT_DEFAULT_ID = abc123...
ℹ AUTH_SECRET = [Key Vault ref — skipped]
ℹ ENTRA_CLIENT_ID = [Key Vault ref — skipped]

✔ Written to .env.local (12 variables)
⚠ 2 Key Vault references skipped. Use --include-secrets to resolve them.
```

### Including secrets

By default, Key Vault references are written as comments. To resolve the actual secret values:

```bash
eai env pull --include-secrets
```

  This requires Azure Key Vault access. You must be logged into the Azure CLI (`az login`) and have the appropriate Key Vault access policy.

### Specifying the environment

Pull configuration for a specific environment:

```bash
eai env pull --env test
eai env pull --env prod
```

### Custom labels

Azure App Config uses labels to scope configuration per application. The CLI detects the label from your `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME` variable, but you can override it:

```bash
eai env pull --label my-custom-app
```

## Listing current variables

View what is in your local `.env.local`:

```bash
eai env list
```

Output:

```
Environment (12 variables)
  AUTH_SECRET = [hidden — use --show-secrets]
  BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API = https://api.example.com
  ENTRA_CLIENT_ID = [hidden — use --show-secrets]
  ENTRA_TENANT_ID = 50808ce0-...
  NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME = trial-portal
  TENANT_DEFAULT_ID = abc123...
```

Secret-like variables (those containing `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `KEY`, `TOKEN`, or `CREDENTIAL` in their name) are masked by default. Reveal them with:

```bash
eai env list --show-secrets
```

## Pushing configuration (admin only)

Push local configuration overrides back to Azure App Config:

```bash
eai env push
```

This updates all values in your `.env.local` in the remote App Config store.

### Push a single key

```bash
eai env push --key BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API
```

### Push with a specific label

```bash
eai env push --label my-custom-app
```

  The push command is intended for administrators. It updates the central configuration that all team members pull from. Coordinate with your team before pushing changes.

## Variable precedence

Variables are resolved in this order, with later sources overriding earlier ones:

1. **Azure App Config** -- the central source of truth, pulled into `.env.local`
2. **`.env.local`** -- your local development overrides
3. **`process.env`** -- system environment variables and shell exports

This means you can override any pulled value by setting it in your shell:

```bash
export BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API=http://localhost:3001
eai resources list Patient  # uses localhost instead of cloud URL
```

## Required variables

These variables must be present for most CLI commands to work:

| Variable                | Purpose                                    | Source          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------|
| `BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API`   | Platform API base URL                      | App Config      |
| `TENANT_DEFAULT_ID`     | Default tenant ID for resource operations  | App Config      |
| `ENTRA_TENANT_ID`       | Entra CIAM tenant ID for authentication    | App Config      |
| `ENTRA_CLIENT_ID`       | Entra app registration client ID           | Key Vault       |
| `AUTH_SECRET`           | Session encryption secret                  | Key Vault       |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME`  | Application name (used as App Config label)| App Config      |

  Run `eai doctor` to check which required variables are missing or misconfigured.

## Multiple environments

You can maintain separate configurations for development, testing, and production. Each environment uses a different label in Azure App Config.

  
    ```bash
    eai env pull --env dev --include-secrets
    ```
    Pulls from the default (dev) label.
  
  
    ```bash
    eai env pull --env test --label trial-portal-test --include-secrets
    ```
    Pulls from a test-specific label.
  
  
    ```bash
    eai env pull --env prod --label trial-portal-prod --include-secrets
    ```
    Pulls from a production-specific label.
  

## Multiple tenants

If your project works with multiple tenants, each tenant ID is stored as a separate variable using the pattern `TENANT_<KEY>_ID`:

```bash title=".env.local"
TENANT_DEFAULT_ID=abc123-def456
TENANT_QUALITY_CONTROL_ID=789abc-012def
TENANT_TRIAL_PORTAL_ID=345ghi-678jkl
```

These map directly to the tenant keys in your `object-types.ts`:

```typescript title="src/eai.config/object-types.ts"
export const objectTypes = {
  'quality-control': [ /* types */ ],  // uses TENANT_QUALITY_CONTROL_ID
  'trial-portal': [ /* types */ ],     // uses TENANT_TRIAL_PORTAL_ID
};
```

## The .env.local file

The generated `.env.local` file includes metadata comments:

```bash title=".env.local"
# Auto-generated by `eai env pull`
# Source: appcs-demo-eai-dev (label: trial-portal)
# Generated: 2025-01-15T10:30:00.000Z
#
# WARNING: Do NOT commit this file.

BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API=https://api.example.com
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_NAME=trial-portal
TENANT_DEFAULT_ID=abc123-def456
# AUTH_SECRET= # Key Vault reference — use --include-secrets to resolve
```

  Never commit `.env.local` to version control. It may contain secrets. The `eai init` command adds it to `.gitignore` automatically.

## Prerequisites

The `eai env pull` and `eai env push` commands require the Azure CLI:

```bash
# Install Azure CLI
brew install azure-cli    # macOS
# or
curl -sL https://aka.ms/InstallAzureCLIDeb | sudo bash  # Linux

# Log in to Azure
az login
```

If the Azure CLI is not installed or not authenticated, the CLI will display:

```
✗ Azure CLI not found or not logged in. Run `az login` first.
```

## Command reference

| Command              | Description                                  |
|----------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `eai env pull`       | Sync cloud config to `.env.local`            |
| `eai env list`       | Show current environment variables           |
| `eai env push`       | Push local overrides to cloud (admin)        |

### Flags

| Flag                 | Command   | Description                              |
|----------------------|-----------|------------------------------------------|
| `--env <name>`       | `pull`    | Target environment (dev, test, prod)     |
| `--label <label>`    | `pull`, `push` | App Config label override           |
| `--include-secrets`  | `pull`    | Resolve Key Vault secret references     |
| `--show-secrets`     | `list`    | Show secret values (default: masked)     |
| `--key <key>`        | `push`    | Push a single key instead of all         |

- [Troubleshooting](/eai-cli/guides/troubleshooting/) -- diagnose environment variable issues with `eai doctor`
- [Deployment](/eai-cli/guides/deployment/) -- configure CI/CD with environment-specific settings
- [Security](/eai-cli/guides/security/) -- manage API keys and secrets securely

# Deployment

The `eai deploy` command automates your CI/CD pipeline. It generates a GitHub Actions workflow, configures the required secrets, triggers deployments, and checks their status -- all from the terminal.

## How it works

```
eai deploy setup     Generate workflow + list secrets
       │
       ▼
.github/workflows/deploy-demo.yml
       │
  git push / eai deploy trigger
       │
       ▼
GitHub Actions  ──→  Build  ──→  Azure App Service
```

The generated workflow:
1. Checks out your code
2. Installs dependencies and builds your application
3. Packages the Next.js standalone output
4. Authenticates with Azure using federated credentials (OIDC)
5. Deploys to Azure App Service via `az webapp deploy`

## Setting up deployment

1. **Generate the workflow file:**

   ```bash
   eai deploy setup
   ```

   This creates `.github/workflows/deploy-demo.yml` in your project. If the file already exists, it is skipped.

2. **Configure GitHub secrets:**

   Pass your GitHub repository to configure secrets interactively:

   ```bash
   eai deploy setup --repo your-org/your-repo
   ```

   The CLI lists the required secrets:

   | Secret                            | Description                           |
   |-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
   | `AZUREAPPSERVICE_CLIENTID`        | Azure AD app client ID for deployment |
   | `AZUREAPPSERVICE_TENANTID`        | Azure AD tenant ID                    |
   | `AZUREAPPSERVICE_SUBSCRIPTIONID`  | Azure subscription ID                 |
   | `AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP`            | Azure resource group name             |
   | `AZURE_WEBAPP_NAME`              | Azure App Service name                |

3. **Set each secret using the GitHub CLI:**

   ```bash
   gh secret set AZUREAPPSERVICE_CLIENTID --repo your-org/your-repo
   gh secret set AZUREAPPSERVICE_TENANTID --repo your-org/your-repo
   gh secret set AZUREAPPSERVICE_SUBSCRIPTIONID --repo your-org/your-repo
   gh secret set AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP --repo your-org/your-repo
   gh secret set AZURE_WEBAPP_NAME --repo your-org/your-repo
   ```

4. **Commit and push the workflow:**

   ```bash
   git add .github/workflows/deploy-demo.yml
   git commit -m "chore: add deployment workflow"
   git push
   ```

## The generated workflow

The workflow file deploys on every push to `main` and supports manual triggers via `workflow_dispatch`:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/deploy-demo.yml"
name: Deploy my-vertical

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

env:
  APP_NAME: my-vertical
  NODE_VERSION: '20.x'

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: demo
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Build Object Types JSON
        run: npm run build:object-types

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      - name: Package standalone output
        run: |
          mkdir -p deploy/${{ env.APP_NAME }}
          cp -r .next/standalone/. deploy/${{ env.APP_NAME }}/
          cp -r .next/static deploy/${{ env.APP_NAME }}/.next/
          cp -r public deploy/${{ env.APP_NAME }}/ 2>/dev/null || true
          cd deploy && zip -r ../app-content.zip ${{ env.APP_NAME }}

      - name: Azure Login
        uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZUREAPPSERVICE_CLIENTID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZUREAPPSERVICE_TENANTID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZUREAPPSERVICE_SUBSCRIPTIONID }}

      - name: Deploy to Azure
        run: |
          az webapp deploy \
            --resource-group ${{ secrets.AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP }} \
            --name ${{ secrets.AZURE_WEBAPP_NAME }} \
            --src-path app-content.zip \
            --type zip \
            --target-path /home/site/wwwroot/${{ env.APP_NAME }}

      - name: Restart App Service
        run: |
          az webapp restart \
            --resource-group ${{ secrets.AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP }} \
            --name ${{ secrets.AZURE_WEBAPP_NAME }}
```

  The workflow uses Azure OIDC (federated credentials) for authentication, not service principal secrets. This is more secure because no long-lived credentials are stored.

## Triggering a deployment

Trigger the deployment workflow manually from the command line:

```bash
eai deploy trigger
```

The CLI auto-detects your GitHub repository from the `origin` remote. You can also specify it explicitly:

```bash
eai deploy trigger --repo your-org/your-repo
```

### Deploy a specific branch

```bash
eai deploy trigger --branch feature/new-types
```

### Use a different workflow file

```bash
eai deploy trigger --workflow deploy-production.yml
```

## Checking deployment status

View recent deployment runs:

```bash
eai deploy status
```

Output:

```
✔ Recent deployments for your-org/your-repo
  ✔ Deploy my-vertical (main) — 1/15/2025, 10:30:00 AM
  ✔ Deploy my-vertical (main) — 1/14/2025, 3:15:00 PM
  ✗ Deploy my-vertical (feature/types) — 1/14/2025, 11:00:00 AM
  ⟳ Deploy my-vertical (main) — 1/15/2025, 10:45:00 AM
```

Status icons:
- **checkmark** -- successful deployment
- **cross** -- failed deployment
- **arrow** -- deployment in progress
- **dot** -- pending/queued

Specify a repository explicitly:

```bash
eai deploy status --repo your-org/your-repo
```

## CI/CD integration patterns

### Deployment after Object Type seeding

A common pattern is to seed Object Types before deploying:

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Seed Object Types
    run: npx @eai-tools/cli types seed
    env:
      BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API: ${{ secrets.BASE_URL_PUBLIC_API }}
      TENANT_DEFAULT_ID: ${{ secrets.TENANT_DEFAULT_ID }}

  - name: Build and Deploy
    run: npm run build
```

### Multi-environment deployment

Create separate workflow files for each environment:

  
    ```yaml title=".github/workflows/deploy-dev.yml"
    name: Deploy (Dev)
    on:
      push:
        branches: [develop]
    jobs:
      deploy:
        environment: dev
        # ... same steps, different secrets
    ```
  
  
    ```yaml title=".github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml"
    name: Deploy (Staging)
    on:
      push:
        branches: [staging]
    jobs:
      deploy:
        environment: staging
        # ... same steps, different secrets
    ```
  
  
    ```yaml title=".github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml"
    name: Deploy (Production)
    on:
      push:
        branches: [main]
    jobs:
      deploy:
        environment: production
        # ... same steps, different secrets
    ```
  

### Validate before deploy

Add validation as a prerequisite job:

```yaml
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20.x'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx @eai-tools/cli types validate

  deploy:
    needs: validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # ... deployment steps
```

## Prerequisites

The deployment commands require:

- **GitHub CLI (`gh`)** -- for triggering workflows and checking status. Install with `brew install gh` or from [cli.github.com](https://cli.github.com/).
- **Azure CLI (`az`)** -- used inside the workflow for deployment. Not required on your local machine unless you push environment variables.
- **Azure OIDC federated credential** -- configured on your Azure AD app registration to trust GitHub Actions tokens.

  If the CLI cannot detect your GitHub repository automatically, it will prompt you to use `--repo your-org/your-repo`.

## Command reference

| Command                | Description                                      |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `eai deploy setup`     | Generate workflow and list required secrets       |
| `eai deploy trigger`   | Trigger the deployment workflow                  |
| `eai deploy status`    | Check recent deployment run status               |

### Flags

| Flag                   | Command         | Description                            |
|------------------------|-----------------|----------------------------------------|
| `--repo <org/name>`    | all             | GitHub repository (auto-detected)      |
| `--branch <name>`      | `trigger`       | Branch to deploy (default: `main`)     |
| `--workflow <file>`    | `trigger`       | Workflow filename (default: `deploy-demo.yml`) |

## Next steps

- [Environment](/eai-cli/guides/environment/) -- configure environment variables for each deployment target
- [Troubleshooting](/eai-cli/guides/troubleshooting/) -- diagnose deployment and CI/CD issues
- [Security](/eai-cli/guides/security/) -- understand credential management in CI/CD
